posts.content_md:
I have sort of been following succinic acid testing thread in the DCG section but not being a hard core DCG'er it kind of flies over my head. But the basic idea is to shift from short to longer wavelengths by soaking in solutions of succinic or citric acid? Wasn't the citric acid soak also used to shift silver halide holos from green to red?

Being lazy and not wanting to sift through a million posts, could anybody be so kind as to summarize the results in regard to chemical concentrations and times in the baths?

And on another, sort of related front, I have a hazy recollection of the use of dichromate to harden the gelatin of silver halide holograms to make them insensitive to humidty changes; what was the final verdict on that procedure?

Thanks for the help!

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
John took a finished, blue narrowband DCG hologram, re-sensitized the DCG layer with dichromate, exposed it to light in a swollen condition, then reprocessed. The result was a green hologram. (This is according to my memory.) John's theory behind this was that the gelatin was slightly hardened while in the swollen state, and couldn't spring back to its original "blue" size, thus the green result.

I really liked John's theory and experiment. I think there was some discussion on Dave's skypecast regarding these results, and it was suggested that the green shift was due to extra water retention, not because of the dichromate treatment. I think Jeff tried this method, and couldn't get it to work (Jeff, please correct me if I'm wrong). I think John stuck to his original argument/experiment. So there seems to be some difference of opinion regarding John's method.

Actually I adopted John's basic idea to explain what was going on with the succinic acid/DCG (though I may be wrong), but instead of "hardening" the swollen layer, I prefer to use the term "rigidize." I don't think the gelatin is becoming hardened with citric or succinic acid, becasue it seems that with washing out, the layer goes back to normal.

The citric acid seems to be very suitable for shifting silver halide holograms after exposure (see the results by Paulos and Ron in the "pseudocolor with green laser" thread).

Tony did some work with citric acid on DCG, and although the shift was greater (as opposed to succinic) the results seemed a bit erratic, plus the holograms appear to be prone to vanishing with citric for some reason.

With the succinic acid, Tony gives the details in his recent thread (regarding concentrations, time in microwave, time and temperature in conventional oven, etc.).

posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md:
Ed,

For Agfa (Millimask): ~90 grams of Citric Acid per liter of water. For VRP-M: ~65 grams per liter. 

I soak the plates (without light) for 30 minutes, squeegee and air dry. This to shift green to amber. This is a reversabe process and if I don't like the color I resoak in water and alter my Citric Acid concentration.

> **Ed Wesly:** Thanks, that's what I was looking for. What was the final result of the dichromate bath to make it humidity proof?

Hi Ed, This is a reply I posted to Ron Olsen Apr 07 07.

"Ron you need of course to minimize ANY color shifting with respect to

your display location and the suggestions of our forum colleagues so far

(would deal with the immediate problem OK possibly but then would cause red shifting when humidity happened to rise or if the sealing up suggestions start to fail.

The answer I think is to thoroughly post harden the gelatin for ever. So put a test hologram in a solution of ~5% ammonium dichromate,

squeegee off excess drips, blow dry it ,and leave it out in sunshine all day.

(If you leave it like this without rinsing it will be extremely resistant to any

future print out but it might be prudent to rinse out any soluble salts since they are poisonous etc..)

This post hardening procedure will cause some final but permanent contraction so you would just need to do tests to compensate by adjusting the swelling state for your initial laser exposure of course.

My tests on this method allowed the pictures to be viewed in or out of water. So your customers could then view the holograms underwater in their swimming pools !"

Pot dichromate would work the same. 

Jeff
